If so, consider locating the refrigerant leak and fixing it or determining whether it makes sense to replace the equipment before its end of life. Do you have equipment that is nearing its end of life? What happens to the equipment at the end of life? Is the remaining refrigerant in retired equipment recycled or thrown away? If you have equipment nearing end of life, evaluate replacements that use refrigerants consistent with your goals. Also consider equipment based on the volume of refrigerant—different configurations of equipment will use different amounts of refrigerant. It is common to replace equipment at end of life. Examples of equipment that are typically replaced include ice makers, refrigerators, and other small, self-contained equipment, all of which are available with a variety of refrigerants. If that equipment has field installed refrigerant lines (such as split systems), the refrigerant lines may need to be replaced or flushed if the new equipment uses a different refrigerant. 9 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Much of the system design and its form factor can be done as a long-term planning process such that when equipment fails, a replacement plan is available that makes implementation easier. For HVAC equipment, verify that the equipment is properly sized. Oversizing equipment (which traditionally has been done for many installations) will yield decreased efficiencies, increased capital costs, and short cycling that increases maintenance costs, in addition to requiring larger quantities of refrigerant. It also can cause humidity control issues. When replacing assets, investigate system configurations that use less refrigerant. Much of the system design and its form factor can be developed as a long-term planning process such that when equipment fails, a replacement plan is available that makes implementation easier. Do you have equipment that uses refrigerants that are not hydrocarbons or carbon dioxide? If yes, develop a disposal plan to be implemented at the equipment end of life. When the equipment fails, having a solution mapped out makes decisions easier at a critical time. 10 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Other Resources Larger systems with ODP refrigerants require federal reporting. Limiting these refrigerants during the planning process will minimize these reporting requirements. Federal reporting requirements10 include that: • Owners or operators of appliances that contain 50 or more pounds of ozone-depleting refrigerant must keep servicing records documenting the date and type of service as well as the quantity of refrigerant added. • Owners or operators must maintain records of the leak inspections and tests performed to verify repairs of leaking appliances. • Owners or operators must submit a report to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency for any appliance containing 50 or more pounds of ozone-depleting refrigerant that leaks 125% or more of the full charge in a calendar year.
